analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give workers 90 days' advance warning before plant closings and mass layoffs.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have extended layoff notice from 60 to 90 days and covered many more employers, was introduced in June 2022 with one cosponsor and died in the House Education and Labor Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already requires large employers to warn workers 60 days before a plant closing or mass layoff, but the rule covers fewer employers than it sounds like and companies have found ways around it. This bill would have extended the warning period to 90 days, covered smaller employers (50 or more employees, or a $2 million payroll), counted remote workers, held parent companies and corporate clients responsible when they make layoff decisions, and added extra damages when employers skip the notice. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers facing a plant closing or mass layoff, who would get three months of pay and warning instead of two — time to find a new job, start training, or arrange unemployment and health benefits. The bill also covers many more workplaces than current law, counts remote workers, and makes parent companies and clients financially responsible when the direct employer dodges notice. Communities and local governments would get earlier, public notice of looming layoffs through a new federal database.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing plant closings and mass layoffs

how_it_helps.text: Bars an employer from ordering a site closing or mass layoff until 90 calendar days after written notice to affected employees, the Labor Department, the governor, and the state's rapid-response dislocated-worker unit.

Expands coverage to employers with 50 or more employees (including part-timers) or a $2 million annual payroll, counts remote workers assigned to a closed site, and lowers the mass-layoff threshold to 10 employees at a single site or 250 company-wide.

Adds liquidated damages equal to 30 days of back pay for violations, extends the deadline to sue to 4 years, and lets states, local governments, and worker representatives enforce the law, not just individual employees.
Holds parent companies, affiliates, and contracting companies that control layoff decisions liable for notice failures, closing routes companies have used to avoid WARN obligations.

Requires a public Labor Department database of layoff notices and bars employers from requiring workers to sign away their WARN rights in severance agreements, except through an attorney- or union-negotiated settlement.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that close sites or conduct mass layoffs, which would carry affected workers on the payroll for an extra month, pay liquidated damages of 30 days' back pay for violations, and cover legal exposure for parent companies, affiliates, and contracting clients that make layoff decisions. The added costs fall hardest on businesses that are already shrinking or failing.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers conducting closures and mass layoffs

drawbacks.text: The bill would roughly extend required paid notice from 60 to 90 days and apply it to much smaller employers (50 employees or a $2 million payroll), raising costs for businesses that are already failing or closing.

It would extend liability to parent companies, affiliates, and even clients of independent contractors that participate in layoff decisions, which could expose entities with limited day-to-day control to lawsuits and damages.
Adding liquidated damages equal to 30 days of back pay and a 4-year window to sue would increase litigation exposure for employers, a cost that an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and concrete: ninety days of notice gives workers time to line up new jobs, training, or unemployment benefits, and stronger penalties make the notice meaningful rather than optional. The main costs fall on employers already in financial distress, and a ninety-day paid notice obligation is substantially heavier than the current sixty, which could push some marginal employers to close sooner or shrink more cautiously. The bill's broad definitions of employer liability (parents, affiliates, and even clients of contractors) go further than current law and could have produced litigation over who actually controls layoff decisions. On balance, the benefits to workers facing permanent job loss outweigh the compliance costs, though the bill never advanced far enough to be refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in June 2022, got almost no cosponsors, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 17, 2022 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which was its only action.
It attracted only one cosponsor in the seven months before the Congress ended, so it had no path to the House floor.

The bill would have rewritten the WARN Act to require 90 days of notice (up from the current 60), lower coverage thresholds to 50 employees or a $2 million payroll, count remote workers, add liquidated damages, and create a public database of layoff notices.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers planning plant closings and mass layoffs are better off, because they never had to meet the longer 90-day notice period, broader coverage, or added damages. Workers facing layoffs are left with the current 60-day rule, which has weaker coverage and penalties.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew enough support for a vote, so no party breakdown exists; its only two sponsors were both Democrats and no Republican ever signed on.

industries.industry: Large employers (50+ employees or $2M payroll) planning closures or mass layoffs
industries.note: They would owe 90 days of notice and pay instead of 60, owe extra liquidated damages, and face far more situations that trigger the law, including layoffs of as few as 10 people at a site and remote workers. The cost lands hardest on companies that are already shutting down.

industries.industry: Parent companies, private-equity owners, and corporate clients of contractors
industries.note: The bill would make entities that control or finance layoff decisions liable for notice failures even when the direct employer is a subsidiary or contractor, removing a common way to avoid WARN liability.

The bill routes new duties and information through these programs: earlier notice, on-site access, labor-management committees, and mandatory public disclosure. It would expand their role in helping laid-off workers find reemployment and training services.
